title: Xherdan Shaqiri: My game in my words
content:
“This is for sure my talent.”

Xherdan Shaqiri is watching a goal he scored for Switzerland against Honduras at the 2014 World Cup, trying to explain how he shoots with such power from a seemingly impossible position.

He cuts inside from the right wing and is faced with three defenders. A fourth is lurking. He has to turn away from goal to escape their attentions. The sensible thing to do would be to play a short pass to a colleague, with a couple of options available. Or he could turn further away from goal and reset the attack. Maybe a slightly more audacious move would be to trick his way out of the jam.

What really doesn’t look on is a shot. With the angle, Shaqiri is probably 30 yards from goal. He’s facing the wrong way and has a defender literally hanging off his arm. Everything is wrong. It looks foolish to even try it.

But he drops a shoulder, manages to vaguely face half goalwards, and with a flex of his hip and a swing of a tree-trunk thigh, he somehow manages to get a shot away. And not just a shot; a rising, thunderous drive into the top corner, kissing the bar on its way in.

From a biomechanical point of view, it looks implausible. It’s not just that Honduras goalkeeper Noel Valladares didn’t get near it; you can tell from his footwork that he was completely unprepared for a shot of any kind, really, let alone of that power.

So how does he do it? The answer is psychological as much as physical, according to the man himself.

“I don’t know if you can learn this,” Shaqiri tells The Athletic. “I always wanted to show myself in this kind of big tournament. For sure, you need the confidence to take the ball, go inside. My left foot is not bad. I trained every day, but this is also a lot about instinct, which is very important.”

Another goal from the Shaqiri archive is ostensibly very different, but required similar instincts. It came in his first season at Stoke, playing away at Everton.

Bojan Krkic plays a pass over the top of the Everton defence for Shaqiri to run onto, which he does at full pelt, his legs whirring like a cartoon. Again, rather than stopping, or checking, or trying to control the ball, Shaqiri meets the ball on the half-volley — still sprinting at top speed — and gently lifts the ball over Tim Howard, who knew he was cooked from the moment Shaqiri touched the ball.

To the outside observer, taking the shot first time looks like an outrageous risk, a recipe for looking silly. But for Shaqiri, the opposite is true. Or at least, he doesn’t think of risk in the same way.

“You can see how difficult it is normally to take one touch,” he says, watching the goal. “Everybody thought that I was going to pass. To have it drop like that, it needed to be perfect over the goalkeeper.

“I’m a player who risks probably a lot in the final third. Maybe 10 times you don’t score, but maybe this is the night. That’s my mentality. If you never try, you’re never going to score. This is what I live every day, and on the field.”

He learned this attitude from his first big transfer. “When I moved from Basel to Bayern, it was the first time in my life I saw (up close) the best players in the world. You have to compete with players like Franck Ribery and Arjen Robben. I took a lot of things from them.”

Shaqiri’s habit of shooting at a time the goalkeeper might not expect showed itself in a goal he scored at Euro 2024, against Scotland.

Anthony Ralston plays a loose pass that Shaqiri — who is playing as a false nine in Switzerland’s 3-4-3 system, lurking behind the Scottish defensive line — is able to intercept…

… but again, many players might take a touch before shooting. Shaqiri, however, hits it first time, taking Angus Gunn by surprise and simultaneously opening up more of the goal to aim at as the Scotland keeper is out of position.

“This was the most important thing for me,” he says. “I saw the ball coming slowly from the defender — it was perfect for me to take one touch. It was just a perfect shot for me to shoot in the near post, and the curve was amazing. It was one of the most beautiful goals I’ve scored. Nobody could save this one.”

Shaqiri has had a slightly odd career. In some ways, he has followed a traditional arc for a leading player from outside the “big five” European leagues. Start with your hometown club, get a big move, win some trophies, and then, when time does its thing, you go somewhere for a last big payday. Then, if the stars align, you come home for an emotional last hurrah.

He began at Basel, then went to Bayern Munich, then Inter, Stoke City and Liverpool, before a stint in MLS at Chicago Fire (via a brief stopover in Lyon), finally coming home to Basel with a bag full of medals — four league titles and a couple of Champions Leagues from Bayern and Liverpool, sundry other trophies and a pretty impressive highlights reel.

But he filled a slightly unusual role at the biggest of those three clubs: never really a first-choice player, rarely one who would start the biggest games, but sometimes a decisive one, particularly in his first season at Anfield.

And particularly for his country, which is where probably his most famous and perhaps best goal came, at Euro 2016, when Switzerland faced Poland in the first knockout round.

The Swiss are a goal down going into the last 10 minutes, when Stephan Lichtsteiner appears on the left flank and hits a slightly hopeful ball into the box. It bounces up off forward Eren Derdiyok and loops towards the edge of the area, just behind Shaqiri.

“We were behind and we had to push in the second half. Usually Stephan was the right side, but at that moment he crossed, the ball came. I was thinking, ‘Let’s try something’.”

That something was a remarkable bicycle kick, caught perfectly on his left foot and sent into the bottom corner, bouncing beyond the grasp of Polish goalkeeper Lukasz Fabianski.

“It was really special and probably the best goal I ever scored.

“Sometimes I just think, ‘I have to try this’. I like to take a risk. Maybe nine or 10 others, they try something different than me. I did this. It makes me unpredictable.”

He also introduced himself to Liverpool supporters, after he signed for them in 2017, with a similarly spectacular overhead kick. This was only in a pre-season friendly during their tour of the United States, but it was against Manchester United, and Shaqiri thinks it was an important way to introduce himself to his new fans.

“For me, to make the change to Liverpool and straight away in America, in my first game, to score this kind of goal… it was perfect. I think you know and you can see that in this moment that from the first day I was feeling at home, and that the fans liked me a lot.“

While he wasn’t a regular most of the time at Liverpool, he did play a key role in perhaps the greatest night at Anfield of the last few years, when they came back from 3-0 down to beat Barcelona in the second leg of the 2019 Champions League semi-final. Shaqiri provided the cross for Gini Wijnaldum to level the tie, after which Trent Alexander-Arnold’s quick thinking set up Divock Origi for the winner.

Shaqiri was only playing because Mohamed Salah and Roberto Firmino were injured. “I know my quality and I knew that I can play also like them. I wanted to come in and to show myself and to show everybody I’m also here and to help the team.

“I don’t know if there’s ever going to be a team like that in Liverpool. I’m also very proud to have been a part of this team.”

A big grin spreads across his face as he watches the clip of the Wijnaldum goal.

“It was probably the best comeback ever: I know Liverpool had one in the final in Istanbul, but this one… this one was incredible, to play against Barcelona with Messi and Suarez. Everybody thought that we were going out. We just believed. We believed in training, we believed before the game.

“The first thing was to make a good performance, and then step-by-step (we got back into it), and then it’s 2-0 and everybody believes. You have to believe in the end, and then you can achieve these kinds of things. If you never give up, nothing is impossible.

“The best thing also was after the game, singing ‘You’ll Never Walk Alone’ — it was a special, emotional moment.”

After leaving Liverpool, Shaqiri had a short spell at Lyon before moving to Chicago, signing with some fanfare in 2022. However, his time in MLS didn’t go to plan to say the least, with disappointing performances from both him and the team, and by 2024, it was time to come home. How does he reflect on his two and a half seasons in MLS?

“It was a really good experience from my side (living in America), but the sport aspect was a bit difficult because we had not the best team in the league, and the pressure on me was high as a designated player. Most of the time I did my work, but I needed more quality in my team, which we didn’t have. So in the end, I was happy to come back to Europe. It was, I think, a perfect time to come back to Basel.”

“There’s a different fan culture in America. There is more pressure in Europe. In America, if you don’t play well, or you don’t win one game, nobody writes to you on social media, nobody is waiting for you at the training ground, you know what I mean?

“I think this is also what I wanted more, to have back this kind of pressure in European football, where you have to win every weekend. That’s the main reason why I came back, because I wanted a new challenge again.”

A new challenge he got, last season helping Basel to their first Swiss Super League victory since 2017, with Shaqiri scoring a hat-trick inside nine minutes in the game that virtually sealed the title, away at Lugano. “That was one of the best drives home I ever had in my life. We were singing all the way back. It was a really special day.”

His form for Basel has fueled talk that he might come out of international retirement for this summer’s World Cup. And although he leaves the door very, very slightly ajar, it doesn’t sound likely.

“It’s helped me a lot to retire from the national team. You know how many games we have now: it’s crazy. It’s like leaving a second job. It was, for me, the right choice to do at the right time.

“I want to see this World Cup as a fan, as a tourist, as a pundit maybe, but I just wanted to see it from outside. I’m really proud of my national career. It’s always like this when you have a good year with your club: people are asking about you. I always get questions like this. Never say never, but at this moment I don’t see a comeback.”
